bigPicture: The sell-off in AI-linked shares deepened overnight: the S&P 500 fell 1.9% on Monday and Asian markets followed on Tuesday, with Korea's Kospi closing below 5,000 for the first time since February, as investors waited for Nvidia's results tonight. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said AI could speed up growth but warned that disappointment could hit jobs and stocks, while markets expect a US rate rise in December. Around the Strait of Hormuz Iran reported several tankers hit by mines and a third US aircraft carrier arrived, yet oil fell 3.6% on expectations of a supply surplus. Russia struck Kyiv's two main bridges, killing two people and cutting heating and water, while Ukraine hit the Crimean Bridge again, as Donald Trump began an Asia trip in Manila. Beyond markets, Africa CDC warned that Congo's Ebola outbreak is still out of control, five EU countries announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, and in Poland the central bank froze the Constitutional Tribunal's payments.

glossary.def: The total stock-market value of a company: share price times the number of shares.

glossary.def: A company's own forecast of its future revenue or profit, which investors compare with results.

glossary.def: The average or median forecast of analysts or economists for a company result or data release.
glossary.example: The consensus for UK unemployment was 4.7%; the actual figure was 4.6%.

glossary.def: A survey measure equal to the share of respondents reporting an increase plus half of those reporting no change; 50 means no change.
glossary.example: Poland's manufacturing PMI, a diffusion index, rose to 50.0 in October.

glossary.def: A statistical method that removes regular calendar patterns (holidays, weather) from data so months can be compared.
glossary.example: US monthly CPI changes are reported seasonally adjusted.

glossary.def: The range within which the true value is likely to lie, because a survey measures only a sample.
glossary.example: The ONS says UK unemployment is accurate to about ±0.3 percentage points.

glossary.def: An early, quick estimate of a statistic based on incomplete data, later replaced by a final figure.
glossary.example: Poland's October CPI flash estimate of 3.5% was confirmed in the final release.

glossary.def: Using warships to stop ships from entering or leaving a country's ports.

glossary.def: Under new EU rules, a centre outside the EU to which people whose asylum claims were rejected can be sent.

glossary.def: A conventional explosive packed with radioactive material, designed to spread contamination and fear rather than cause a nuclear blast.

glossary.def: Finding and monitoring people who were near an infected person so new cases are caught early.

glossary.def: The share of people with a confirmed disease who die from it.
glossary.example: WHO put the crude case fatality rate in Congo's Ebola outbreak at about 49%.

glossary.def: A government's budget balance excluding interest payments on its debt.

glossary.def: A grouping of the US, Australia, India and Japan that cooperates on security in the Indo-Pacific.
glossary.example: Trump meets Quad leaders in Manila this week.

glossary.def: An armed group organised like an army but not part of a country's official armed forces.

Early on Tuesday Infineon was down 0.5%, Reuters reported, as Washington tightened restrictions on AI chip sales to China. stocks.overview: Chip and AI-linked shares led the falls: on Monday Nvidia dropped 4.1% before its results tonight, Micron and Intel about 7%, and on Tuesday Samsung Electronics, SoftBank Group and Advantest fell 3–4% in Asia, while TSMC lost 2%. In Europe, ASML and Siemens fell on Monday, and on Tuesday morning Deutsche Bank slid about 5% after reports based on leaked documents. Warsaw's big stocks were mostly steady on Monday, with KGHM down 3.3% as metal prices weakened and the GPW exchange operator up 5.5% after strong results; Tyson Foods and Telus jumped on company news in New York.

stories.everyday: Many pension funds and ETFs that Poles hold through PPK or IKE accounts own large US tech shares, so their value moves with these swings. Korean, Japanese and Taiwanese chip firms also make parts for phones and computers sold in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: The fall in AI-linked shares is cutting the value of the world's largest companies and pension savings tied to them, and it spread from Wall Street to every major Asian market.
stories.title: AI sell-off spreads: S&P 500 falls 1.9%, Kospi drops below 5,000 as Nvidia reports tonight
stories.what: On Monday the S&P 500 closed at 7,416.59 (−1.9%), the Nasdaq Composite at 24,509.76 (−2.5%) and the Dow at 51,608.17 (−1.4%). Nvidia fell 4.1%; AP says it has lost about $735 billion in market value since disclosures about former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week. On Tuesday Asian markets followed: AP reported the Kospi down 2.6% to 4,968.48, its first close below 5,000 since February, the Nikkei 225 down 1.3% and Australia's ASX 200 down 1.8%, while India's Sensex edged up. Nvidia reports its quarterly results after the US close on Tuesday (around 22:20 Warsaw time), the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.
stories.why: Investors had bid up chipmakers and AI companies on expectations of years of fast growth; when doubts appear (here the leadership crisis at Nvidia and new US curbs on chip access), the most expensive shares fall hardest. AP also points to worries about an AI bubble and to Democrats, who gained in the midterm elections, possibly favouring limits on new data centres. Nvidia guided for quarterly revenue of $108 billion (±2%) and Bloomberg's consensus is about $109.1 billion, according to Saxo, so the outlook for next quarter is what investors will watch most.

stories.everyday: Oil prices feed into what Poles pay for petrol, diesel and heating within weeks; a lower Brent price helps, but new attacks can reverse it quickly.
stories.rankWhy: Hormuz carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war, so attacks on tankers there threaten energy supplies and prices for most countries.
stories.title: Tankers hit by mines and a projectile around Hormuz as a third US aircraft carrier arrives; oil still falls 3.6%
stories.what: Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy said mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday on routes it calls unauthorised, and Iran's regular navy reported another tanker fire on Tuesday, which it called the fourth such incident in under 24 hours; the claims could not be independently verified. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) separately reported a tanker disabled by an attack about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, and another hit by a projectile while leaving the strait; no casualties were reported. A US official said the carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has arrived, the third US carrier in the region, as a US naval blockade of Iranian shipping continues. Despite this, Brent crude settled down 3.6% at $92.44 a barrel on Monday.
stories.why: The US–Israeli war with Iran began on 28 February and has been in a stalemate for months; talks have stalled over Iran's nuclear programme and Iran's demand that the US first lift the blockade, AP reports. Oil fell because traders focus on supply overall: the International Energy Agency (IEA) expects a surplus in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover, and Chinese refinery runs fell, Reuters reported. Lloyd's List says Hormuz traffic is still below a third of pre-war levels, so the risk of a renewed price spike remains.

stories.everyday: Attacks on Ukraine's energy system can push more Ukrainians to seek shelter abroad in winter, including in Poland, and keep defence spending high across the region.
stories.rankWhy: Strikes on bridges and heating in a city of about three million in winter, plus a hit on Russia's supply route to Crimea, raise the stakes just before leader-level talks in China.
stories.title: Russia hits Kyiv's two main Dnipro bridges, killing two; Ukraine strikes the Crimean Bridge again
stories.what: A combined Russian drone and missile attack overnight damaged Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro, mayor Vitali Klitschko said; traffic on both was suspended and water and heating supplies were disrupted. Kyiv's military administration said two people were killed in the Obolonskyi district. Crimea's Russian-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said Ukraine attacked the 19-km Crimean (Kerch) Bridge for a second day and traffic was halted; Ukraine has not officially claimed it and the extent of damage is unverified. Russia's defence ministry said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones over 22 regions, which it called the largest Ukrainian drone attack of the war, according to The National; a Reuters report carried by RTÉ cited Russian statements that nearly 200 drones were downed overnight, so tallies differ by period.
stories.why: Bridges carry supplies and people: Russia's strikes on Kyiv's crossings and power grid hit civilian life in winter, while the Crimean Bridge is the main land link supplying Russian forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine. The National notes that both sides are escalating before Vladimir Putin travels to the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where a three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping is planned and Trump has said Ukraine will be discussed.

stories.everyday: Higher US rates tend to lift the dollar against the złoty, making dollar-priced goods such as fuel and electronics a bit dearer in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The Federal Reserve sets the cost of dollar borrowing for the whole world, and markets now expect it to raise rates in December.
stories.title: Fed chair Warsh says AI could speed growth but warns a disappointment could hit jobs and stocks, as markets price a December rate rise
stories.what: Speaking at a Fed conference on AI and productivity in San Francisco on Monday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said AI appears to be changing the speed of innovation and could keep growth well above its long-run average. He also warned that if returns on AI infrastructure spending fall short, stocks could drop steeply and unemployment could rise; he did not discuss inflation or the next rate move, AP reported. The CME FedWatch tool showed a 100% probability of a December rate rise as of 12 November, after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report; the next Fed decision is due on 9 December. The US 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.13% on Tuesday in Asia, from 5.15%.
stories.why: When inflation runs above target, a central bank raises interest rates to cool borrowing and spending. Expectations of higher US rates strengthen the dollar and raise the return on safe bonds, which is one reason gold, which pays no interest, fell to around $3,855 an ounce on Tuesday, near a one-year low, according to Mitrade. Several Fed officials blame the data-centre building boom for part of the price pressure, AP says.

stories.everyday: US–China relations shape prices of electronics and the health of global trade, which matters for Poland's export-driven factories.
stories.rankWhy: Trump's Asia trip leads to a planned first three-way meeting with Xi and Putin on nuclear weapons and to trade deals affecting several large economies.
stories.title: Trump lands in Manila for ASEAN and the first Quad leaders' meeting of his term, before the APEC summit in China
stories.what: President Donald Trump arrives in Manila on Tuesday for the ASEAN summit, the first stop of his Asia trip and his first trip abroad since his party's losses in the midterm elections, AP reports. He is due to meet the leaders of the Quad (US, Australia, India, Japan) and to sign a trade deal with Thailand; on Wednesday Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. hosts him with full military honours. He then travels to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit, where a three-way meeting on nuclear weapons with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin is planned. ASEAN leaders are also negotiating a non-aggression pact with China over the South China Sea.
stories.why: The Quad is a grouping that the US uses to counter China's influence in the Asia-Pacific, so meeting it just before visiting China is a balancing act. Under an October framework, Thailand would remove tariffs on most US goods and spend over $18 billion on US aircraft, AP says, after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's earlier 19% tariff on Thailand in February.

stories.everyday: Shipping disruption in the Red Sea makes Asia–Europe deliveries slower and dearer, which can feed into prices of goods in European shops.
stories.rankWhy: A Houthi push towards Aden and the Bab al-Mandeb strait threatens a key shipping lane and millions of people in a country already in a humanitarian crisis.
stories.title: Yemen: government reports 661 attacks on the Houthis as it reinforces Aden; parliament labels the group 'terrorist'
stories.what: Yemen's army said it carried out 661 attacks on Houthi positions, including 15 air strikes, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as part of its 'Dawn of Yemen' offensive launched on 5 October, Al Jazeera reported. Government-aligned forces are repositioning to defend Aden, the government's temporary capital, after pulling back from positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait when the Houthis cut a supply route along the Red Sea coast; AFP sources put Houthi forces about 60 km from Aden on Sunday. The UN says more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in July, The New Arab reported. Yemen's parliament unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a terrorist organisation; it now goes to Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi.
stories.why: Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean; whoever controls its coast can threaten ships heading to and from the Suez Canal. The terrorism law allows prosecution and asset freezes, which aims to choke off Houthi finance and arms supply, according to the state Saba agency.

stories.everyday: The risk to people in Europe is assessed as low by health agencies, but outbreaks like this show why disease surveillance and aid budgets matter far beyond Africa.
stories.rankWhy: The second-largest Ebola outbreak on record has killed more than 5,500 people and the African Union's health agency warns it could spread to more countries.
stories.title: Africa CDC: Congo's Ebola outbreak is still out of control six months on, with more than 5,500 deaths
stories.what: Six months after the outbreak was declared in May, Africa CDC said the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo is still not under control, Reuters reported at the weekend; government data show more than 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths. The US CDC calls it the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, after West Africa in 2014–16. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which the WHO says there is still no approved vaccine or specific treatment; a trial of candidate vaccines began in Congo on 23 October. Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria, according to WHO and CDC data.
stories.why: Africa CDC says more than 80% of new cases come from people outside known contact lists, meaning the virus is spreading unseen; it cites attacks on health workers, staff unpaid for months and a lack of resources. Of about $2.9 billion pledged, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya urged donors to release around $1.6 billion, warning of spread to the Central African Republic and South Sudan.

stories.everyday: Staff pay and invoices at the Tribunal may go unpaid while the dispute lasts, and the row adds to uncertainty about how constitutional complaints by citizens are handled.
stories.rankWhy: A central bank freezing payments of the country's top constitutional court deepens Poland's institutional dispute and raises questions about the NBP's independence.
stories.title: Poland's central bank halts all payments from the Constitutional Tribunal's accounts
stories.what: The National Bank of Poland (NBP) stopped carrying out all payment orders from the Constitutional Tribunal's accounts, spokesman Maciej Antes said, after the bank's legal department found grounds to do so. The step followed a letter from Tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski to NBP governor Adam Glapiński asking him to block the accounts for people claiming the right to manage the Tribunal; the NBP said it cannot settle who runs the court. Finance Minister Andrzej Domański said the NBP 'should conduct monetary policy, not politics' and that the government would look at other ways to fund the Tribunal. Separately, the President's Chancellery said it would present a combined proposal on the Tribunal on Tuesday after talks that KO and the Left did not attend.
stories.why: The Tribunal is at the centre of a long political dispute in which rival camps claim the right to run it, and the NBP says it cannot judge between them. Government figures see the freeze as political: Jan Grabiec, head of the Prime Minister's Chancellery, accused PiS of using its appointees, including President Karol Nawrocki and NBP governor Glapiński, to block the Tribunal, money.pl reported.

stories.everyday: The case is a reminder for parents and schools that extremist recruitment increasingly happens in online chats used by teenagers.
stories.rankWhy: Poland's internal security agency says it stopped teenagers linked to an international neo-Nazi network from preparing a bomb attack, highlighting online radicalisation of minors.
stories.title: Poland's ABW detains three teenagers accused of preparing a bomb attack for a neo-Nazi network
stories.what: The Internal Security Agency (ABW) detained three Polish teenagers, two aged 17 and one aged 16, linked to an international neo-Nazi group that prosecutors in Gdańsk describe as a terrorist organisation, Polsat News reported. One 17-year-old allegedly had a ready pipe bomb and explosive ingredients and was converting an air rifle into a firearm; prosecutors say the 17-year-olds planned to plant a device in a block of flats to attack a specific person. Two were remanded for two and three months and the 16-year-old was placed in a youth shelter. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said these were 'real preparations for an attack', not just online posts.
stories.why: Officials say such groups recruit young people through messaging apps, spreading hatred of Jews, migrants, Black people, LGBT people, politicians and police. Special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak pointed to an ABW report on the radicalisation of young people.

stories.everyday: How Europe handles migration affects labour markets, public budgets and politics across the EU, including in Poland, which borders the EU's eastern frontier.
stories.rankWhy: Five EU countries plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, a test of new EU rules that rights groups say could breach migrants' rights.
stories.title: Five EU countries plan a 'return hub' in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers from 2027
stories.what: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands announced at a migration conference in Vienna that they plan to open a centre in Rwanda in 2027 for people whose asylum claims were rejected and who cannot be returned to their own countries. Diplomatic sources told AFP it would start as a pilot for about 100 people, and the Dutch government said the first phase would involve only single men. Deportees could stay in Rwanda or go back to their home country. Human Rights Watch said Rwanda has a poor rights record and that no human rights assessment was published; Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez criticised the plan.
stories.why: The EU's new Return Regulation allows member states to set up 'return hubs' outside the EU. Governments say the aim is to ease pressure on asylum systems and break smugglers' business; Frontex counted almost 110,000 irregular border crossings in the first ten months of 2026, 29% fewer than a year earlier.

stories.everyday: Poles working in the UK feel hiring conditions there directly, and UK interest rates set the cost of mortgages and loans for anyone borrowing in pounds.
stories.rankWhy: The UK jobs data feed directly into whether the Bank of England raises interest rates again, which affects millions of mortgage holders.
stories.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly falls to 4.6%, but payrolls and vacancies drop
stories.what: The UK unemployment rate fell to 4.6% in the three months to September, down 0.3 points on the previous quarter and below forecasts of 4.7% (the previous release), the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday; it is the lowest since the three months to April 2025. The number of unemployed people fell by 88,000 to 1.684 million and employment rose by 155,000. However, the number of employees on company payrolls fell by a provisional 34,000 in October, vacancies dropped to 690,000 (the lowest outside the pandemic since 2014) and regular pay growth slowed to 3.5% from 3.7%, ActionForex reported. The ONS said part of the fall reflects the rotation of its survey sample, and the estimate has a margin of error of about 0.3 points either way.
stories.why: Mixed jobs data make the next interest-rate decision harder: a lower jobless rate suggests a tight labour market that can push wages and prices up, while falling payrolls and vacancies suggest cooling demand. UK inflation data for October are due on Wednesday.

stories.everyday: Cheaper Chinese cars entering Western markets add competition for European carmakers and their suppliers, many of which have factories in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A G7 country deepening trade ties with China on the eve of APEC shows how US allies are hedging, with effects on farmers and carmakers.
stories.title: Xi and Carney agree more Chinese tariff cuts for Canada as APEC gathers in Shenzhen
stories.what: Chinese President Xi Jinping met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Shenzhen on Tuesday, before the APEC summit. China will cut tariffs on about C$400 million of additional Canadian exports, including frozen pork, fish and seafood, and Canada will extend by two years its tariff relief on some Chinese steel and aluminium, Reuters reported. Ottawa has already approved annual imports of 49,000 Chinese cars at a 6.1% tariff, rising to 70,000 over five years.
stories.why: Canada is trying to reduce its dependence on the US market, aiming to raise exports to China by 50% by the end of the decade; Carney said relations now have 'greater predictability and stability'. Critics cite security concerns and Chinese interference in Canadian elections found by Canadian intelligence.

stories.everyday: Political change in Serbia, an EU candidate country, may affect the pace of EU enlargement in the Western Balkans, which Poland generally supports.
stories.rankWhy: Serbia's first parliament with a student-led majority meets, ending 14 years of dominance by Aleksandar Vučić's camp in an EU candidate country.
stories.title: Serbia's new parliament meets for the first time after the student movement's landslide win
stories.what: Serbia's newly elected parliament holds its first session on Tuesday, about three weeks after the Student List won 140 of 250 seats in the October election, RFE/RL reported. Its first task is to elect a speaker, who will also act as president, since Aleksandar Vučić resigned as president in June; a presidential election must be held by the end of the year. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the first sitting, and the movement has not yet named candidates for prime minister or speaker.
stories.why: The Student List grew out of two years of mass protests demanding accountability for the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. It promises to fight corruption and organised crime and to protect the independence of courts and the media.

stories.everyday: Escalation risk in the Gulf feeds into oil prices and so into fuel costs in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Reported US intelligence on Iranian plotting against senior officials in Washington could shape decisions on whether the war with Iran escalates again.
stories.title: US intelligence reportedly indicates Iran is drawing up plans to target officials in Washington with a 'dirty bomb'
stories.what: Citing seven US officials, CNN reported that new intelligence suggests Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a 'dirty bomb' (a conventional explosive that spreads radioactive material) or a chemical weapon. The sources said the planning appears to be about building options and does not point to an imminent attack, and officials disagree over whether Iran has the capability or intent. The White House said there are 'no credible threats', WION reported. Separately, Vice President JD Vance said President Trump would not let the conflict become a 'forever war'.
stories.why: Such reports can raise pressure on the administration to strike again, at a time when US and Israeli planners are reportedly drawing up options and a third US carrier has arrived, Gulf News reported.

stories.everyday: Climate deals shape EU energy rules and carbon costs, which feed into Polish electricity and heating bills because Poland still relies heavily on coal.
stories.rankWhy: Nearly 200 countries must agree by Friday on how fast to move away from fossil fuels and how much to pay poorer nations to adapt.
stories.title: COP31's first draft deal offers two options on fossil fuels as talks enter their final days
stories.what: Negotiators at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, published an 18-page draft deal on Monday that offers two options on fossil fuels: repeating the 2023 language on 'transitioning away' from them, or a more ambitious 'phase out'; either could be dropped, Reuters reported. The draft also shows disagreement over Turkey's proposal to raise electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035 and over how much rich countries should give poorer ones for adaptation. Australia's Chris Bowen, who leads negotiations under a split presidency with Turkey, said he expects strong feedback. The talks are due to end on Friday 20 November.
stories.why: Agreements at UN climate talks require consensus, so oil-producing and fossil-fuel-dependent countries can block strong language. A UN report last month found the world is already on course to exceed the 1.5°C warming threshold.

stories.everyday: Mostly a matter for shareholders and regulators for now; the bank says it does not expect a meaningful financial impact.
stories.rankWhy: A sharp fall in a major German bank after a large leak raises reputational and regulatory questions, with limited wider spill-over so far.
stories.title: Deutsche Bank shares drop about 5% after a media leak of 15 million records on dealings with oligarchs, Trump and Epstein
stories.what: Deutsche Bank shares fell about 5% in early trading on Tuesday (5.04% by 09:09 Warsaw time, 5.2% in early trade per another Reuters report) after a consortium of journalists published reports in Der Spiegel, the Financial Times and the New York Times based on 15 million leaked records. The reports describe the bank's dealings with clients including Russian oligarchs, President Donald Trump and the late financier Jeffrey Epstein; Reuters could not immediately verify them. The bank said the incidents 'date back many years', some up to two decades, that it has improved its controls and that it does not expect a meaningful financial impact. The Stoxx 600 fell 0.64% to 658.07, with chipmakers such as ASML (−1.32%) also lower after the new US chip curbs.
stories.why: Banks depend on trust and on regulators' confidence in their controls against money laundering and sanctions breaches; reports of past failings can raise the risk of fines or investigations, so investors sell first and wait for details.

stories.everyday: Sudan's war is one of the world's largest displacement crises, adding to refugee flows towards North Africa and Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Another deadly air strike on civilians in Sudan's war, which has displaced about 13 million people.
stories.title: Sudan: rights groups say an army drone strike killed at least 13 civilians, including children, in West Kordofan
stories.what: A strike on Sunday on the Abu Qalb area of Abu Zabad locality in West Kordofan killed at least 13 people, mostly women and children, according to the rights group Emergency Lawyers, which blamed the Sudanese army, AP reported. The Kordofan Human Rights Observatory put the toll at 15, including four children killed on a football field, Radio Dabanga reported; the figures could not be independently verified. A spokesperson for forces fighting alongside the army said troops had 'eliminated' positions of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in the area.
stories.why: The army and the RSF have been at war since April 2023; aid groups say at least 59,000 people have been killed and drones have become the deadliest threat to civilians, AP reports.

stories.everyday: Crime is one of the main concerns of South Africans and a frequent warning in travel advice for visitors.
stories.rankWhy: Two mass shootings highlight South Africa's high level of violent crime, which weighs on communities and investment.
stories.title: South Africa: two separate mass shootings kill 17 people
stories.what: Police in South Africa said on Monday that two separate shootings had killed at least 17 people: eight people found dead in a bullet-riddled vehicle at Sweetwaters outside Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal, and nine people found shot dead in a shack in the Jeffsville informal settlement near Pretoria, AP and allAfrica reported. Police say motives have not been established and no arrests have been made. AP notes earlier mass shootings this year that police linked to criminal gangs, including 12 people killed in Johannesburg in June.
stories.why: Police have not established motives for these attacks; AP reports that several earlier mass shootings were linked by police to criminal gangs.

stories.everyday: Such incidents show how Russia's tensions with the West reach well beyond Europe.
stories.rankWhy: An airspace violation adds tension between Japan and Russia days before both leaders attend the APEC summit.
stories.title: Japan scrambles fighter jets after two suspected Russian aircraft violate its airspace
stories.what: Two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Okinoshima, an island off Fukuoka, shortly after 4 a.m. on Tuesday, each staying about three minutes, AFP reported. Japan scrambled fighter jets and lodged a 'very stern protest'; Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara called the violation a grave infringement of sovereignty and 'completely unacceptable'. South Korea and Taiwan reported separate Russian military flights the same day.
stories.why: Relations have worsened since Russia arrested a Japanese journalist in October and seized Japan Tobacco's assets in Russia, AFP notes; Japan's last such protest was in 2024.

stories.everyday: A reminder to keep a backup way to pay, such as a card from another bank or some cash.
stories.rankWhy: Online banking problems at several of the largest US banks briefly affected thousands of customers, days after a nationwide air-traffic outage.
stories.title: Thousands of customers report online outages at major US banks, including Chase
stories.what: Customers of JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, US Bank and the Zelle payment service reported problems logging in, seeing balances and moving money on Monday, according to Downdetector; Chase had nearly 5,000 reports, Al Jazeera reported. A Chase spokesperson blamed 'a technical issue' and said customers still had access to their accounts; CNBC, citing a source, said 'bad actors' did not appear to be involved.
stories.why: Large banks rely on shared technology providers and payment networks, so one fault can spread to many institutions at once; no cause had been published for the other banks.

stories.everyday: Brazil is a major exporter of food such as soy, coffee and beef, so its economic stability matters for global food prices.
stories.rankWhy: Brazil's attempt to calm investors about its public finances after the election affects Latin America's largest economy.
stories.title: Brazil's Senate votes on contested changes to Lula's 2027 fiscal bill
stories.what: Brazil's Senate was due on Tuesday to vote on four contested amendments to bill PLP 299/2026, the 2027 fiscal package backed by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, after approving the main text 45–31 on 12 November, The Rio Times reported. The bill would cap real spending growth at 2% instead of 2.5% in years of fiscal restraint and cut company tax breaks by up to 20%; official estimates put the improvement in the primary budget balance at 45–56 billion reais, while BTG Pactual estimates 27.9 billion. It then goes to the Chamber of Deputies.
stories.why: After Lula won a fourth term in the 25 October runoff, the real fell 12% against the dollar and stocks dropped nearly 14% on worries about spending, and public debt has risen to about 11.1 trillion reais, AP reported.

stories.everyday: Much of the world's gold supply chain starts in small, informal mines, which raises questions about where jewellery and investment gold come from.
stories.rankWhy: A crackdown on informal gold mining affects the livelihoods of thousands of West African migrants and strains regional relations.
stories.title: Guinea bans illegal gold mining in Siguiri and arrests more than 1,200 miners
stories.what: Guinea has banned illegal gold mining in its northeastern Siguiri region and arrested at least 1,263 suspected miners, including nationals of Burkina Faso, Mali, Togo, Nigeria, Ivory Coast and Ghana, allAfrica reported. Authorities cite environmental protection and better regulation of the sector; critics allege mistreatment and deportations, and Burkina Faso and Mali have raised concerns. The crackdown coincides with the start of operations at Guinea's first gold refinery in Conakry.
stories.why: Authorities say the aim is to protect the environment and better regulate the sector; the crackdown coincides with the start of operations at Guinea's first gold refinery.

stories.everyday: Aid budgets are decided by taxpayers' governments, including the EU's, so these choices are shaped by voters in donor countries.
stories.rankWhy: Falling aid is leaving refugee children in Bangladesh and Ethiopia more exposed to trafficking and child labour.
stories.title: UNHCR and Oxford University warn aid cuts are exposing refugees to trafficking and child labour
stories.what: UNHCR and Oxford University warned that falling humanitarian funding is leaving refugees in Bangladesh and Ethiopia more vulnerable to trafficking, child labour and exploitation, allAfrica reported. More than 170,000 Rohingya refugees have arrived in Bangladesh since 2024, where shelter and water conditions have worsened, and in Ethiopia planned child-protection needs were only 18% funded in 2025. The organisations called for more predictable funding.
stories.why: When funding falls, agencies cut services such as child protection, which leaves families more likely to send children to work or to accept risky offers from traffickers, the organisations warn.

stories.everyday: Power cuts in Iraqi Kurdistan hit homes and businesses directly as winter approaches.
stories.rankWhy: Repeated drone threats to Iraqi Kurdistan's main gas field affect electricity supply for millions in the region.
stories.title: Drone over Iraq's Khor Mor gas field sets off sirens a week after an attack halted output
stories.what: Warning sirens sounded in Iraq's Kurdistan region on Monday after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field, Reuters reported citing two security sources; no strike or damage was reported. Production at the field was already halted the previous week after a suspected drone attack caused a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of power generation, according to the UAE-based operator Dana Gas.
stories.why: Khor Mor supplies much of the gas used for electricity in the Kurdish region; Kurdish officials have blamed Iranian-backed armed groups for repeated attacks, Al Jazeera reported.

stories.everyday: Violence in the West Bank shapes EU policy debates on Israel and the Palestinians.
stories.rankWhy: Violence around a new settler outpost near Jericho wounded both Palestinians and Israelis, part of a wider pattern of West Bank clashes.
stories.title: West Bank: Palestinians wounded by settler gunfire and Israelis hurt in an attack near Jericho
stories.what: A Palestinian woman and man were wounded by gunfire from settlers in a neighbourhood near Jericho that settlers took over earlier this month, according to Haaretz and Palestinian media; the Palestine Red Crescent said the woman was shot in the head and is in critical condition, the Times of Israel reported. Separately, two Israelis were lightly wounded outside Jericho when, according to Hebrew media, Palestinian assailants rammed their vehicle and attacked them with axes. The Israeli army set up roadblocks in the area.
stories.why: The incidents are linked to a new settler presence near Jericho, which has raised tensions between settlers and Palestinian residents.

stories.everyday: Consolidation among telecom companies can affect phone and internet prices for consumers, which is why regulators review such deals.
stories.rankWhy: A possible takeover of one of Canada's three big telecom groups would reshape a national market, but it faces regulatory hurdles.
stories.title: Telus confirms an unsolicited takeover proposal from Québecor; its shares jump 12%
stories.what: Canadian telecom group Telus confirmed on Monday that it received an unsolicited, non-binding proposal from rival Québecor to buy it, which Bloomberg valued at about C$31 billion; an amended offer on 9 November raised the share component to 0.17 Québecor shares per Telus share, Telus said. Telus's board said it is not satisfied the offer reflects the company's value, citing regulatory and execution risk, a governance structure that would give Québecor's controlling shareholder voting control, and higher debt. Telus shares rose 12.37% on Monday in New York, according to StockTitan.
stories.why: Because the share part of the offer uses a fixed exchange ratio, Telus holders would bear swings in Québecor's share price during a long regulatory review, the board said; the share jump suggests investors see a chance of a deal or a higher bid. A special committee is reviewing the proposal and other strategic options.

stories.everyday: Drug approvals in the US often set the pace for access to new treatments elsewhere, including in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: The FDA's rejection delays a closely watched new type of lung-cancer drug in the US and hit the developer's shares.
stories.title: US FDA declines to approve Summit's lung-cancer drug ivonescimab for now; shares fall 16%
stories.what: The US Food and Drug Administration issued a complete response letter, meaning the application cannot be approved in its present form, for Summit Therapeutics' ivonescimab with chemotherapy in a type of advanced non-small cell lung cancer in patients previously treated with EGFR inhibitors, the company said. The FDA said a benefit in progression-free survival without a statistically significant improvement in overall survival does not support approval. Summit shares fell 16.47% on Monday, StockTitan reported.
stories.why: Regulators usually want proof that a cancer drug helps patients live longer, or a clear benefit-risk balance, before approval; the trial showed a positive trend in survival that did not reach statistical significance, Summit said. The company will continue other trials with partner Akeso.

stories.everyday: A new Bond film is likely to be one of the most-watched cinema releases in Poland when it arrives; no release date has been given.
stories.rankWhy: A major cultural announcement for one of the world's best-known film franchises, with little wider effect.
stories.title: Robert Pattinson is named the next James Bond
stories.what: Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that British actor Robert Pattinson will play James Bond in the next 007 film, to be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight. Pattinson called the role 'the honour of a lifetime', the studio said.
stories.why: Bond films are among the most valuable film franchises, so the casting matters commercially for Amazon MGM Studios, which made the announcement.

stories.everyday: Shows how housing shortages lead to informal building in fast-growing cities.
stories.rankWhy: A local housing decision that protects some residents of Zimbabwe's capital for now.
stories.title: Harare suspends all housing demolitions until further notice
stories.what: Harare City Council has suspended all housing demolitions until further notice; Acting Town Clerk Warren Chiwawa told all departments to stop demolitions unless his office authorises them, allAfrica reported.
stories.why: The memorandum gives no reason; demolitions usually target structures the city considers built without permission.

stories.everyday: Little direct effect on daily life in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: India's leader used the ASEAN summits to stress stability; symbolic, with no new agreements reported yet.
stories.title: Modi tells the ASEAN-India summit in Manila the world needs 'peace, stability and predictability'
stories.what: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is in Manila for the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit, focusing on maritime cooperation, trade and security, WION reported. In his address he said the world needs 'peace, stability and predictability'.
stories.why: The summit week also includes a Quad leaders' meeting, which AP describes as aimed at countering China's influence in the Asia-Pacific; India is a Quad member.
